q: Why should test data be kept separate from model training and tuning?
a: It provides an independent estimate of generalization. Using it to choose the model leaks information into the evaluation.
explanation: Split according to the real prediction setting: time, entities, or groups may matter. Repeated test-set tuning can make the reported score optimistic even if model fitting never directly sees those rows.
mistake: Treating a random row split as correct for every dataset.
followups: What if users appear in several rows?
When should you use a time split?

q: A classifier is 99% accurate on data with 1% positive cases. Is it useful?
a: Not necessarily. An always-negative classifier can reach that accuracy; inspect precision, recall, errors, and the decision cost.
explanation: Choose a baseline and metrics tied to the task. Evaluate threshold behavior and minority-class performance. The best threshold depends on false-positive and false-negative consequences.
followups: How do precision and recall trade off?
When is a PR curve useful?

q: A model performs much worse after deployment than in cross-validation. How could preprocessing leak information?
a: Preprocessing fitted on all data can expose validation information. Fit transformations only on training data within each evaluation fold.
explanation: Use a pipeline so scaling, imputation, and feature selection respect the split. Also inspect future information and duplicate entities. Compare with a leakage-free baseline before adding complexity.
mistake: Applying fit_transform to the whole dataset before splitting.
followups: How should production transforms be reused?

q: Design validation for an incoming analytics dataset.
a: Check schema, key uniqueness, null/range rules, freshness, and distribution changes before making it available.
explanation: Distinguish hard contract failures from warnings. Record input versions and rejected records so failures are traceable. Do not silently replace corrupt values with defaults that change business meaning.
mistake: Treating a successfully parsed file as valid data.
followups: How do you handle late records?

q: Design monitoring for a deployed prediction model.
a: Monitor data quality, feature distributions, inference failures and latency, and outcome quality when labels become available.
explanation: Distribution changes do not always mean performance degradation. Track segments and label delays, compare meaningful baselines, and define rollback or retraining decisions with owners.
mistake: Retraining automatically after every detected input shift.
followups: How do you handle delayed labels?

q: How would you evaluate an assistant that answers questions using retrieved documents?
a: Separate retrieval quality from answer quality and test grounding, unsupported claims, access permissions, latency, and useful refusal behavior.
explanation: Build a representative versioned evaluation set with difficult and unanswerable cases. Trace which material was retrieved and used. More context is not proof of a better or authorized answer.
mistake: Judging the system only by fluent wording.
followups: How do you update stale documents?
What if a retrieved document contains instructions?

q: Choose which business workflow should receive an ML feature first.
a: Compare user value, data availability, measurable baselines, failure cost, and operating requirements before committing.
explanation: A simple rule may be sufficient. Define human oversight, evaluation ownership, and rollback. Track actual workflow outcomes and error costs rather than only a model score.
mistake: Selecting a project because the model technology is fashionable.
followups: When should a human review predictions?

q: Design reproducible model training for several teams.
a: Version data, transformations, code, configuration, and evaluation artifacts, and record how a released model was produced.
explanation: Match training and inference feature semantics and control access. Provide repeatable environments and ownership of data contracts. Reproducibility includes dependencies and input provenance, not just a random seed.
mistake: Saving only model weights and calling the process reproducible.
followups: How do schema changes affect models?
